result.title: Phosphoproteomics profiling of the monocytes uncovers the mechanosensory pathways regulating monocytes responses to pathologic level of shear stress
result.authorString: Lai AL, Chheang C, Fang H, Danish H, Mirzaalikhan Y, Dayawansa N, Watson A, Noonan J, Ang C, Greening D, Peter K, Baratchi S.
result.abstractText:
Background:

Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is the most common valvular heart disease in older adults and currently has no approved pharmacological therapy to prevent or slow disease progression. Aortic valve replacement, either surgically or by transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), therefore remains the only effective treatment for severe CAVD. Monocytes play an important role in driving inflammation and disease progression in CAVD. As the disease progresses and the aortic valve becomes increasingly stenotic, circulating monocytes passing through the narrowed valve are repeatedly exposed to pathological haemodynamic forces, including markedly elevated shear stress, before their recruitment into the valve tissue. However, how exposure to these mechanical forces reprograms circulating monocytes influences their subsequent responses within the valve remain poorly understood.

Methods and Results:

In this study, we used an engineered model of aortic valve stenosis combined with phosphoproteomic profiling to investigate how prolonged exposure to pathological shear stress reprograms circulating monocytes and influences their subsequent phenotype and function following recruitment into the valve matrix. We further used TAVI as a unique clinical model to determine whether restoration of physiological haemodynamics in patients with severe aortic stenosis reverses the shear-induced monocyte phenotype observed in our experimental model. We found that prolonged exposure of monocytes to pathological shear stress induced extensive remodelling of the proteomic and phosphoproteomic landscape, with enrichment of pathways associated with cellular metabolism, cytoskeletal organisation, and inflammatory signalling. Kinase activity analysis further identified increased protein kinase C (PKC) activity accompanied by suppression of AKT signalling. Consistent with these molecular changes, pathological shear stress increased actin polymerisation, mitochondrial membrane potential, intracellular calcium signalling, and PKC activity. Using a bioengineered extracellular matrix model that recapitulates the glycosaminoglycan-rich microenvironment of the stenotic aortic valve we found that prior exposure to pathological shear stress altered monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation, reducing oxidised LDL uptake and foam-cell formation while promoting co-expression of CD80 and CD163, indicative of a mixed macrophage phenotype. Finally, using a myeloid-specific Piezo1 knockout mouse model, we identified Piezo1 as a key mechanosensor linking pathological shear stress to PKC activation, mitochondrial responses, and persistent changes in monocyte phenotype following migration into the extracellular matrix.

Conclusions:

These findings establish a mechanistic link between abnormal valve haemodynamics, metabolic and inflammatory reprogramming of circulating monocytes, extracellular matrix remodelling, and immune dysregulation during CAVD progression, highlighting monocyte mechanotransduction and downstream PKC/Piezo1 signalling as potential therapeutic targets.

result.title: Stiff guidewire entrapment by mitral chordae during transcatheter aortic valve replacement without worsening of mitral regurgitation: a case report
result.authorString: Lyu Z, Hong B, Luo X.
result.abstractText:
Background: In transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), a stiff guidewire provides left ventricular support but can inadvertently engage the mitral subvalvular apparatus. This may provoke acute mitral regurgitation (MR) and circulatory compromise. Case presentation: A 71-year-old woman with symptomatic severe calcific aortic stenosis underwent transfemoral TAVR under general anesthesia. Baseline transthoracic echocardiography showed mild MR, a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 30%, a peak aortic jet velocity of 4.82 m/s, and a mean aortic valve gradient of 53 mmHg. A 24-mm VitaFlow Liberty valve was implanted over a preshaped stiff guidewire. After valve deployment, the guidewire could not be withdrawn from the left ventricle. Blood pressure decreased transiently; however, immediate transthoracic echocardiography showed mild MR without apparent worsening. The wire was then carefully retrieved with coaxial support from a multipurpose catheter. Visual inspection of the retrieved wire revealed a tissue fragment consistent with chordal tissue within its distal coil. MR remained mild on postoperative day 1 and at 2 months. At the 2-month follow-up, LVEF had improved to 47%, left ventricular dimensions had decreased to 51/39 mm, and transcatheter valve function was normal.

Conclusions:

Unexpected resistance when removing a ventricular stiff guidewire after TAVR should raise concern for mitral subvalvular entrapment. Immediate hemodynamic evaluation and echocardiography should direct management. Catheter-supported retrieval may be considered only when MR is not worsening and the patient is stable; deterioration warrants prompt multidisciplinary rescue planning.

result.title: The Generalizability Gap in Aortic Stenosis: Analysis of 87 Clinical Trials vs. Real-World Practice
result.abstractText: Background: Randomized trials guide the selection of transcatheter and surgical aortic valve replacement, but their applicability depends on how closely enrolled participants resemble patients treated in routine practice. We evaluated the demographic generalizability of contemporary interventional aortic stenosis trials and examined whether representativeness differed between transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). Methods: We systematically analyzed interventional aortic stenosis trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Eligible studies reported structured baseline data on participant age and sex and had a mean participant age greater than 40 years. Trials were classified by intervention type using study titles, intervention descriptions, and procedural terminology. Enrollment-weighted mean age and female representation were calculated and compared with published aggregate data from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database, which served as the real-world reference population. Results: Of 103 identified trials, 87 met the inclusion criteria and enrolled 26,526 participants. Across all included trials, the weighted mean age was 78.6 years, and 44.1% of participants were women, compared with 81.5 years and 48.0% women in the reference population. Among 45 TAVR trials, the weighted mean age was 81.3 years, closely approximating real-world practice. In contrast, participants in 10 SAVR trials had a weighted mean age of 75.5 years, approximately six years younger than the reference population. TAVR trials also outnumbered SAVR trials by more than four to one. Conclusions: The demographic generalizability of aortic stenosis trials differs substantially by intervention type. TAVR trials enrolled patients whose ages more closely reflected contemporary practice, whereas SAVR trials enrolled considerably younger populations. This generalizability gap may limit the direct application of surgical trial outcomes to older, potentially more vulnerable patients, particularly women. Greater attention to demographic representativeness is needed when interpreting comparative evidence, developing guidelines, and counseling patients regarding valve-replacement strategies.
